key_insight: In a large academic medical center, researchers identified a small but real pattern of “AI psychosis,” most often where AI interactions amplified existing delusional thinking.
clinical_relevance: The finding suggests clinicians should ask about AI use when assessing psychosis, especially in first-episode cases and when symptoms seem newly reinforced by chatbot conversations.
method: Searched Vanderbilt EHR notes for AI-related keywords from 12/1/2022 to 4/1/2026.
Included only records with psychosis as the primary diagnosis and reviewed notes by three raters.
Classified AI interactions into four predefined types: Catalyst, Amplifier, Co-Author, and Object.
evidence_signal: Out of 73 eligible patients, 28 were rated as AI psychosis, 17 as neutral AI interactions, and 28 as AI-themed delusions without documented chatbot use.
watch_item: This was a single-center EHR study based on note review, so documentation quality and keyword capture may limit how broadly the findings generalize.
paper_title: Characterizing artificial intelligence (AI) psychosis in a large academic medical setting: evidence of the new clinical phenomenon and the vulnerability of those in early phases of psychosis
